HETDEX · satellite streaks · an AI-assisted workflow

Crowded skies,
AI-powered science

By the end of our astronomical survey, satellites streaked across more than one in five HETDEX observations in some months. AI gave me the extra hands to find out which satellites they were.

Erin Mentuch Cooper · November 2026

Photo: one hour of satellites over the northern Atacama Desert in Chile, 15 October 2025, above the dome of ESO’s Extremely Large Telescope. Credit: F. Kamphues, ESO/M. Kornmesser (CC BY 4.0).

“Satellites now outnumber the visible stars above most towns.”

Tereza Pultarova, Space.com, 17 November 2026

The Hobby-Eberly Telescope Dark Energy Experiment (HETDEX) used the 10 m Hobby-Eberly Telescope and spent 2017–2024 taking spectra of the sky to map over a million Lyman-alpha emitting galaxies at 1.9 < z < 3.5 and measure dark energy. Over those same years, the number of satellites overhead exploded.

As a research scientist and data manager for the survey, I noticed more and more satellites crossing our data as time went on. At first we thought we could ignore them. They didn’t create emission lines, so they weren’t obvious contaminants in our sample. But as their numbers went up, it became clear they were becoming stronger contaminants: they leave excess continuum light across our IFUs, create false positives in our catalog, and block our deep view of the sky.

I’ve worked in extragalactic astronomy most of my life, and I knew little about these polluters of our sky. I had no choice but to try to become an expert. This is where AI helped me enter a field I knew very little about, and my use of AI changed over time as LLMs burst onto the scene. This page walks through the complete workflow: how we found the streaks, masked them, published them in our public data, measured them, and finally worked out which satellite made each one.

6,778observations in HETDEX Public Data Release 1
527satellite streaks in 492 observations
7.3%of observations contaminated; above 20% in some months of 2023–24
90.1%of streaks matched to a catalogued object (475 of 527)
0.09%of the survey area lost to the satellite mask

Numbers from Mentuch Cooper et al. 2026, AJ 172, 303.

The problem
01

A survey built to see a million faint galaxies

HETDEX reduction pipelineVIRUS on the 10 m HET

HETDEX observed with VIRUS (the Visible Integral-field Replicable Unit Spectrograph), a set of integral-field units (IFUs) on the 10 m Hobby-Eberly Telescope at McDonald Observatory in West Texas. Each IFU is a bundle of 448 fibers, each 1.5″ across, and the focal plane holds up to 78 of them spread over a ~22′ field. Because fibers cover only part of the sky, every observation is three dithered exposures of about six minutes that fill in the gaps between fibers.

The goal was to detect over a million Lyα-emitting galaxies (LAEs) at 1.9 < z < 3.5 and use their clustering to measure the expansion history of the Universe. The survey design, reductions and detections are described in Gebhardt et al. (2021).

448fibers per IFU, 1.5″ each
3dithers per observation
3500–5500 Åspectral range
Gebhardt et al. 2021, ApJ 923, 217Hill et al. 2021: the HET upgrade and VIRUSHobby-Eberly Telescope
02

Continuum detections with no counterpart

Line + continuum detectionELiXer forced photometryVisual inspection

The reduction pipeline produces both emission-line and continuum detections. The catalog is then filtered to group and clean detections (Mentuch Cooper et al. 2023). Every detection is compared with forced photometry in deep imaging that complements our spectra.

Some continuum detections had no obvious counterpart in that imaging at all. Plotted across the focal plane, they lined up. It quickly became apparent these were satellites: you can even see one crossing five IFUs in Figure 3 of the survey paper, labeled “most likely an asteroid or satellite.” They produced false positives in our catalog and blocked our deep view of the sky.

Mentuch Cooper et al. 2023, ApJ 943, 177
Detect & mask
03

RAIC labels the satellite detections

RAIC (RAIC Labs, AI for Impact program)Human-in-the-loop labeling

We used RAIC, a visual AI search platform from RAIC Labs, through their AI for Impact program. RAIC classified spectrally collapsed 20″ × 20″ image cutouts (4000–5000 Å) around every continuum detection. Starting from a single example image, RAIC returns similar images across the whole dataset; we accept or reject them, and the classifier improves with each correction.

Detections scoring above 0.3 for the “satellite” label were flagged. Any observation with at least five satellite-labeled continuum detections became a streak candidate. The same approach labeled meteors and instrumental artifacts.

“RAIC allowed us to do the work of a much, much larger team.”
Erin Mentuch Cooper, in RAIC Labs’ write-up of the project
raiclabs.comAstronomers aim to measure dark energy with assist from RAIC
04

A straight line through the detections, fit by hand

Manual fithetdex_api track list

A satellite crosses the focal plane in a straight line, so each streak is a linear fit to the flagged detections in sky coordinates. These fits were done manually: an observation can contain spurious detections, more than one satellite, or a meteor, and any of those can drag an automatic fit off the real track.

The fits are stored as a track list in the hetdex_api repository, one line per observation and exposure (shotid expnum slope intercept). Every later step, including the orbital cross-match, starts from this list.

05

Mask ±6″ around every track

Catalog maskingInternal fiber data model

For our catalogs, we mask any detection that falls within 6″ of the fitted line, measured perpendicular to the track: a 12″-wide strip. Later we masked all fiber data along the same strip in our internal data model.

The mask is deliberately conservative and often removes more area than strictly needed. Even so, the streaks cost only 0.09% of the survey area.

Open data
06

The mask travels into the public datacubes

PDR1 datacube pipelineSAT mask bit 1024

For HETDEX Public Data Release 1 we built a final database of IFU datacubes and the HETDEX Source Catalog 2. The fiber-level satellite flag was interpolated (nearest neighbour) into each cube’s mask extension as the SAT bit, 1024, “on a known satellite track.”

Detections use all three dithers combined, so a satellite seen in one dither is masked in all three. Anyone using the cubes can remove satellite light with (mask & 1024) == 0, or keep only it, which is exactly what the next steps do.

431,713IFU datacubes in PDR1
546satellite streaks masked

07

Teaching Claude the data

Tutorials written by handClaude in Jupyter AITACC JupyterHub

From the PDR1 paper I wrote a series of twelve tutorial notebooks, dexcube, covering the data model, downloading cubes, masking options, collapsing cubes, extracting spectra and querying the catalog.

From those tutorials I built a full LLM context (HETDEX_CONTEXT.md and CLAUDE.md): survey parameters, the cube format, every mask bit, data paths and the mistakes people commonly make. Users of our public JupyterHub can now ask Claude questions about HETDEX data and have it write code right inside the Jupyter AI environment. A Claude subscription is needed for this to work.

This step is what made the rest fast. Once Claude knew how to read the cubes and their masks, measuring the satellites was a request, not a project.
HETDEX/dexcube on GitHubHETDEX JupyterHub at TACCWatch on Loom
Measure
08

Claude measures every streak

Claude Sonnet 4.5astropy · specliteSpectral review

The satellite light was already flagged in the public cubes, and Claude already knew how to use them, so I asked it to do the measurements. For each flagged IFU it pulled the SAT-masked spaxels (keeping the satellite light while still applying the other quality masks), split observations with more than one crossing using the track list, and summed the spectra. Because a trail appears in only one of three co-added dithers, the flux is corrected for that dilution. It then measured g-band magnitude, surface brightness, the streak endpoints and position angle.

Spectral inspection removed five events that were meteors, not satellites: their spectra show bright emission lines, while satellites show reflected sunlight with the Sun’s absorption lines.

527streaks in 492 observations
5meteors removed
1036wavelength channels per spectrum, 2 Å each
Full record: eriniocentric/hetdex_sats
Identify
09

Which satellite was it? Archival orbits

Claude Sonnet 4.5Space-Track gp_history

Here is where the story gets exciting. I had the spectra, but I didn’t know which satellites made them. I didn’t think I had the time, or the energy, after writing three full papers for HETDEX while no longer employed on the project. This is where Claude stepped in: it helped me cross-match each track with archival two-line element sets (TLEs), the orbital elements that describe where every catalogued object was on a given night.

Choosing the archive mattered. Space-Track’s gp_history holds historical elements for every catalogued object across 2017–2024. CelesTrak’s free service serves only current elements, and SatChecker’s archive starts in July 2019, which would have dropped 55 pre-Starlink streaks: exactly the baseline we needed.

370observing nights of TLEs cached
~25,000objects propagated per observation
10

Propagate every orbit, score every track

Claude Sonnet 4.5 (code)SGP4astropy coordinates

For each observation, SGP4 propagates every catalogued object across the full observation window: start − 60 s to start + 3 × exposure + 240 s + 60 s. A coarse 20-second pass keeps anything near the field, widening each object’s search radius by its own motion so fast low-orbit satellites aren’t skipped between samples. A 0.5-second fine pass follows.

Candidates are scored on three things: the perpendicular offset between the predicted path and the streak, the agreement in position angle, and an along-track timing cut. The perpendicular offset is the key discriminant because TLE errors are mostly along-track: they change when a satellite arrives, not where its path lies. The best match and four runners-up are kept.

Within hours, the cross-matching was done.

475of 527 identified (468 Space-Track + 7 SatChecker)
471unambiguous

0.08°median position-angle residual
Verify

Nothing ships until this passes

A fast answer is only useful if it’s right. Before the paper went out, every identification had to survive four layers of checking: tests and diagnostics built into the pipeline, an independent archive, a blind rebuild by a stronger model, and a deep audit by the newest one.

11pass

Sanity checks and diagnostic figures

Claude Sonnet 4.5 (proposed + coded)Human review of every figure

These are the checks we built into the pipeline. Each one is there because a plausible-looking result can still be wrong.

  • Is it sunlight? Satellite spectra must show the Sun’s absorption lines (Ca H&K, G band, Hβ, Mg b). Emission lines mean a meteor.
  • 82 offline unit tests of the geometry and scoring, plus a regression test for every bug that ever reached the science.
  • Was it really there? An along-track timing cut stops “perfect” matches to an object sitting degrees away on the same great circle.
  • Don’t skip fast satellites. A fixed coarse radius missed 27% of fast crossings; the radius now scales with each object’s motion.
  • Use the true exposure time. A frozen 1,320 s window cut off long observations; fixing it raised matches from 438 to 468.
  • Is it lit? Low-orbit matches must be in sunlight, not Earth’s shadow, at the crossing time.
  • Physics check at GEO. Geostationary tracks should have PA ≈ 90° − inclination: predicted 76.0°, measured 75.2°.
  • Brightness vs. literature. Starlink normalized to 550 km gives g = 5.95, matching the published VisorSat V = 5.92 ± 0.04.
  • The 52 unmatched streaks were searched, not skipped. They have lower S/N (7.7 vs 11.1) and real solar spectra.
  • Is the trend real? Streak rates are corrected for survey cadence: LEO rises ~20×, while GEO changes are consistent with Poisson noise.
  • Visual galleries for all 527 streaks: focal-plane plots, IFU images with mask contours, and predicted vs. measured tracks.
  • Retractions logged. Two claims made along the way (a cos δ correction, and that the high-orbit matches were contamination) were tested, found wrong, and recorded.
1297% agree

SatChecker: a second archive and a second propagator

IAU CPS SatChecker

We cross-checked 180 of our Space-Track identifications against SatChecker from the IAU Centre for the Protection of the Dark and Quiet Sky from Satellite Constellation Interference. SatChecker runs its own SGP4 propagation from its own TLE archive, so agreement tests both our elements and our code.

161 / 166resolved cases agree (97.0%; 95% CI 93.1–98.7%)
12.6″median offset for agreements, vs. 14.0″ in ours

The five disagreements (streaks 407, 410, 445, 467 and 498) are cases where two objects pass close to the same track. The 14 that SatChecker couldn’t resolve mostly predate its archive.

SatChecker

A blind rebuild with a stronger model

Claude Opus 4.8sgp4 + astropy TEME framesFresh Space-Track pulls

The original pipeline was written mainly with Claude Sonnet 4.5. To verify it, I had a stronger model rebuild the identifications from scratch, under written “blind rules”: it was not allowed to read the original matching code or results until the very last step.

  • Downloaded and integrity-checked 90.6 million element sets in 740 files, finding real defects in the archive (bad checksums, a mislabeled record).
  • Propagated with astropy’s satellite frames, validated against an independent library to ≤ 1.5″.
  • Set match tolerances from a physical error budget, then measured the false-match rate with null tests: 2.6% per streak.
  • Only then compared with the published catalog, and investigated every disagreement one by one.

Of the disagreements, three are cases where the independent object fits far better, two are genuinely ambiguous, nine published IDs are probably right but just outside the stricter tolerance, and eight published IDs are questionable.

14open question

A deep audit finds a timing issue

Claude Opus 5.5Raw VIRUS frame headersManual review of the data

The most recent checks, with Claude Opus 5.5, looked at when each dither was taken. Two findings:

A small timing error. The per-dither times in the survey file are stored at single precision, good to only about ±169 s, so the precise time has to come from the date and time strings. The published catalog also assumed each dither starts right after the previous one. Raw frame headers show an extra 15–21 s gap, so our dither 2 and 3 windows open up to ~40 s early. Of 177 fast low-orbit crossings, 10 fall outside every exposure under the published timing and none under the corrected timing. The identifications themselves barely move: crossing times for shared objects agree to a median of 0.12 s.

Too many streaks in dither 1. In early data, satellites appear far more often in the first dither than in the other two. Labels for early data were never set (they defaulted to 1), but the excess remains when the dither is assigned from each orbit’s crossing time, and it remains when I review the data by hand. It doesn’t come from timing, brightness or orbit type. I have no idea yet why that could be.

Results & next
15

What 527 streaks tell us

Analysis + writingGCAT satellite counts
  • 7.3% of observations contain a streak, and monthly values pass 20% by 2023–2024, tracking the number of payloads in orbit.
  • After correcting for survey cadence, the low-Earth-orbit streak rate rises about 20× from 2018 to 2024.
  • Only 35% of identified objects launched since 2010. The rest are spent rocket bodies, debris and older spacecraft: a deep survey sees the whole history of spaceflight.
  • Distant objects are visible because slow trails dwell on each fiber. Geostationary and high orbits make up almost half of the identifications.
  • The 34 Starlink streaks match published VisorSat brightness.
Mentuch Cooper et al. 2026, AJ 172, 303arXiv:2611.10301Catalog + code on Zenodo
16unresolved

Still open

Decisions

The timing offset and the dither-1 excess are not resolved. I decided to leave the published catalog unchanged and carry the corrections into the expanded analysis, and not to quote a “fraction of streaks missed” until the cause is measured. The plan for next time:

  • Take each dither’s shutter times from the raw frame headers.
  • Use one streak-finding method for all dithers and all epochs.
  • Assign dithers from orbital crossing times, with visual labels as a cross-check.
  • Calibrate match limits with offset “control” streaks for each dataset.
  • Measure completeness from predicted crossings, including where tracks thread between IFUs.
17

Next: the parallel VIRUS sky

Future work

Future work will expand the analysis to a much wider set of data taken at the HET. Every time HPF or LRS2 observes, VIRUS takes a parallel exposure of the surrounding sky. I will search that dataset for satellites too, with the lessons from steps 11–14 built in from the start.

Science isn’t perfect. AI will keep expanding and improving with every prompt. Dynamic records of the work can keep it going beyond publication.

Erin Mentuch Cooper

A cross-match I didn’t think I had time for was done within hours. The verification took far longer, and that was the point: each new model and each independent tool found something the previous one missed, and two of those findings are still open.

The catalog is public, the code and the full record of how it was made are on GitHub, and the open questions are written down. That is how the next person, or the next model, picks up where we left off.
